E1502.summary: The reviving spirit of the Phoenix from which, Atwood says, Bacon filled his lamp; the text does not explain it further.
E1502.body: Atwood speaks of Bacon being able to “fill his lamp from her reviviscent spirit” [I.1 ¶38], the spirit belonging to the Phoenix, which he worked by ascending and descending. The passage leaves the expression unexplained; it apparently names a vivifying principle drawn from the Phoenix, but the text gives no plain meaning.

E1503.summary: An Arabian alchemist the book cites for public transmutations, as a master who wrote obscurely, and in the Ordinal for the dietary of the matter.
E1503.body: Atwood names Rhasis as an Arabian alchemist famous for public displays of transmutation [I.1 ¶34]. As “Rasis” he appears in Norton's verse among masters (with Hermes, Geber, Avicen, Morien, Bacon, Raymond and others) who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Within the Ordinal, Rasis is cited as having “set the dietary”: the matter must not eat hastily — “Non tamen comedat res festinanter,” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: yet let the thing not eat hastily). He is also named in Eirenaeus' allegory as read by those sitting in darkness [III.4 ¶16].

E1505.summary: An adept (Richardi Ang. Libel.) cited to support the view that study of the philosophers' writings must precede practice.
E1505.body: Atwood quotes “the adept Ricardus” from Richardi Ang. Libel. cap. 3: “I beg of thee, my son, says the adept Ricardus, to examine the writings of the philosophers” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n16]. She uses him with approval to support her point that study of theory precedes practice and that study overthrows ignorance.

E1506.summary: An adept, author of the Twelve Gates, Medulla and verses to King Edward, whom Atwood cites often on the First Matter, solution, putrefaction and concealment, while criticizing the Gates' disorder.
E1506.body:
Ripley is one of Atwood's most-cited authorities.

**On concealment and honesty.** His Fifth Gate supports her view that a plain art is veiled to protect it from the unworthy: “In horrid metaphors veiled are an art most plain” [I.1 ¶85; I.1 n111]. In his Epistle to King Edward IV he offers, conditionally, to show his king the Stone's working and argues against wilful deceit: “Never trewly for merke nor for pounde Make yt I common” [I.1 ¶79–80; I.1 n105].

**Against ignorant practice.** His Admonition of Erroneous Experiments illustrates the failures of working on vulgar substances: “But profytt found I right none therein.” [I.1 ¶64–65; I.1 n72]. Via Ashmole he is cited for verses against those who prate “Of Robin Hood, and of his Bow” without practice [I.1 ¶64]. Yet Atwood criticizes the Twelve Gates as disorderly and misleading [I.1 ¶62–63].

**On the Matter.** Stanza 10 of the Epistle supports reduction to the first matter: “Without they be reduced to their beginning materiable” [I.2 ¶5–6; I.2 n7]. The Medulla, cap. i, supports that separation and recombination of Mercury's elements make the elixir: “The elements of Mercury being separated” [I.2 ¶25; I.2 n23]. He calls the First Matter a middle or third thing: “Aquosa substantia sicca reperta” [I.2 ¶31, ¶42] (ours: a watery substance found dry). The Admonition supports that man is the mine of the natural mercury: “Out of hy myner by arte yt most be brought” [II.1 ¶13; II.1 n11]. “The Canon Ripley” is among those agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**On the operation.** The Second and Fifth Gates and Ripley Revived illustrate the vapor running down in the vessel, the sun obscured with waters like Noah's flood, and purgation to a white Elixir: “Ryght so to water minerall reduced ys our gold” [III.1 ¶56–62; III.1 n61, n63, n69]; Atwood glosses his phrase “by Crafte occasionate” [III.1 n69]. The consummating Conjunction is “by Ripley called tetraptive” [III.3 ¶33]. In contrast, his attempt to putrefy his Red Salt by alternate heat and cold is called a “singular” method [IV.1 ¶36].

He is listed among genuine seekers, against the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49]; Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): he warns against haste under the similitude of red poppies [APP ¶103].

E1508.summary: Author of De Veritate et Antiquitate Artis Chemiae in the Theatrum Chemicum, cited for the antiquity of alchemy.
E1508.body: Atwood cites Robert Vallensis's De Veritate et Antiquitate Artis Chemiae, in the first volume of the Theatrum Chemicum, in support of alchemy's antiquity [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n4]. A further footnote refers to the same work as a source, closing “Haec ille Andaeas” [I.1 n52] (ours: thus that Andaeas).

E1509.summary: Atwood's expression for that which is so called because it lies in great obscurity and is hard to reach, surrounded by darkness and clouds.
E1509.body: Atwood explains the name herself: “This is the rock in the wilderness,, because in great obscurity and difficult to find the way of” [II.3 ¶30]. It is surrounded by darkness, clouds and exhalations, as though in the bowels of the earth. The text states the reason for the name (obscurity and inaccessibility); what “this” is must be taken from the surrounding passage.

E1510.summary: The ‘experimental Friar’, an adept Atwood cites on concealment, the Matter, solution, the operator's purification and the primacy of understanding over experiment.
E1510.body:
Atwood treats Roger Bacon as a genuine adept who produced gold; Friar Bacon said he saw and touched the perfect thing transmuting [I.1 ¶76]. His maxim justifies concealing the practice: “truth ought not to be shown to every ribald, for then that would become most vile, which, in the hands of a philosopher, is the most precious of all things” [I.1 ¶38–39; I.1 n43, n44]; conscience led him to withhold his gift. His Libro de Mirab. Natur. Operib. contains extracts from Rhasis and appears to credit Artephius's tale [I.1 ¶34, ¶36; I.1 n41].

On method, he supports leaving off experiments until understanding is attained: “operate according to the blood; i.e., according to the understanding” [I.1 ¶86; I.1 n112]. Called “the experimental Friar”, he supports that the beginning is dissolving and investigating the philosophic man: “Volo ovum philosophorum dissolvere et partes philosophici hominis investare, nam hoc est initium ad alia” [II.3 ¶5; II.3 n1] (ours: I will dissolve the philosophers' egg and investigate the parts of the philosophic man, for this is the beginning of the rest). The Radix Mundi and Speculum support that subject-matter, not species, is transmuted, and that the first work is Solution: “Species non transmutantur, sed subjecta specierum optime et propriisime” [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n1] (ours: species are not transmuted, but the subjects of species best and most properly). The Radix Mundi also supports the operator's moral requirements: “it is impossible for you to attain this immortal essentiality, unless you become sanctified in mind and purified in soul” [III.3 ¶28; III.3 n19].

As “the experimentalist” he is agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]; something warned him “from the error of his ways” [IV.4 ¶27]. Norton's verse names “Freer Bacon” with Albertus, and Agrippa followed Friar Bacon's example in proving principles [I.1 ¶60, ¶64].

E1511.summary: In quoted authorities, the one root from which all metals and minerals descend, identified with the metallic seed.
E1511.body: Quoted from Basil and Geber: “all metals and minerals have one root from whence their descent is” [II.1 ¶11]. The same passage equates it with the seed: “this metallic seed, or root” [II.1 ¶11]. The record suggests that this root is also the inner basis the operator must find in himself, though that is the context's implication rather than a stated definition.

E1512.summary: Atwood's term for the source in which Reason is to seek genuine reminiscence.
E1512.body: Atwood says Reason is “to seek for genuine reminiscence in her root of Light” [IV.4 ¶15]. Apparently the same source she elsewhere calls the Root of Reason [IV.4 ¶20], though the text does not equate the two expressly.

E1513.summary: The Source and proper object of the rational faculty, buried in the life of sense and resuscitated by Hermetic Artifice; identified with Wisdom and the saving Salt.
E1513.body: Atwood: “the proper object of the rational faculty is in its Source, which lies profoundly buried in this life of sense” [IV.4 ¶20]; Hermetic Artifice resuscitates it. She identifies it directly: “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20] — so = Wisdom and = saving Salt.

E1515.summary: A secret association, known through the Fame and Confession, into which some adepts carried their work for protection.
E1515.body: Atwood says some adepts carried their work into a secret association, the Rosicrucian Fraternity of the Fame and Confession, for protection [I.1 ¶66]. She also notes that certain Rosicrucians were alarmed by the books of Agrippa's and Paracelsus' disciples [II.1 ¶9].

E1516.summary: A voice cited (Calid in Salmon) for the view that the art belongs to those who understand and cannot be bought or sold.
E1516.body: Atwood cites the royal artist, per the footnote from Calid in Salmon, p. 30: “this treasure is not to be bought with money; and as it cannot be bought, so neither can it be sold” [III.4 ¶18; III.4 n13]. She uses it in support: the art is for those who understand.

E1517.summary: In Urbigeranus and other adepts, that which is extracted from ‘our Sordid Subject’ by the medium the Arcanum shows.
E1517.body: Quoted from Urbigeranus and other Adepts: the Arcanum shows “the medium by which the Royal Diadem may be extracted from our Sordid Subject” [IV.1 ¶7]. The text does not explain the expression further; it apparently names the precious product hidden in the base subject.

E1518.summary: In Flammel, the herb found triumphing at the summit of the mountain of the Seven, called mineral, vegetable or saturnine and being ‘either and all’.
E1518.body: Quoted from Flammel: at the summit of the mountain of the Seven is “a royal herb triumphing, which some call mineral, some vegetable, some saturnine” [II.4 ¶9]; it is said to be either and all. The text gives no plainer gloss.

E1519.summary: Atwood's name for the single path toward which all Hermetic treatises direct once it is found.
E1519.body: Atwood says the Hermetic treatises are “all directing on the same Royal Road when this is found” [III.4 ¶15]. The expression is not otherwise defined here.

E1520.summary: In a quoted adept, that which moved upon the waters, made body in the virgin womb of the greater world, and identified with the Stone.
E1520.body: Quoted from “the mysterious adeptest”: “Ruach Elohim, which moved upon the face of the waters, the firmament being in the midst” [III.3 ¶50]. The same passage has it conceived and made body in the virgin womb of the greater world, and identifies it with the Stone.

E1521.summary: The God-given standard for discerning right from wrong; the superior Reason is called ‘the Reason of our Rule’.
E1521.body: The Alchemists' counsel: “Take hold of that Rule which God hath given thee for direction” [III.1 ¶13]. Atwood links it to the superior Reason: “the superior virtue of that which is the Reason of our Rule” [III.1 ¶21]. Compare Rule of Reason.

E1522.summary: Atwood's term for Reason as guide of the pursuit: under it every step progresses, it alone enters the true Form of Gold, and it proves all things.
E1522.body: Atwood: “every step is progressive where the Rule of Reason is pursued” [III.4 ¶11]; of the true Form of Gold, “Reason alone can enter into it” [III.4 ¶11]. Reason's office is inquiry: “It is the province of reason to inquire and endeavor, by perscrutination, to prove all things” [III.4 ¶15].

E1523.summary: Atwood's term for that Spirit, communion with which is the way to the magistery, and whose Law is to be feared and obeyed.
E1523.body: Atwood presents “communion with the ruling Spirit of nature” [I.3 n19] as the way to the magistery; its Law is to be feared and obeyed.

E1524.summary: An adept named among genuine seekers and cited in support of Basil Valentine's view.
E1524.body: Rupecissa is cited as supporting Basil Valentine's view [I.2 ¶31]. As “Rupicessa” he is listed with De Meun, Flamel, John Pontanus, Basil Valentine, Ripley, Lully and Cremer as genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49].

E1525.summary: The ancients' art practised in the Mysteries, which Atwood connects with Alchemy and Mesmerism and seeks to revive.
E1525.body:
Atwood speaks of the ancients' Sacred Art practised in the Mysteries, comparing it with Mesmerism: “if we connect it with the ancients’ Sacred Art” [II.2 ¶7]. She says her chapter aimed “to indicate the connection of the Sacred Art and Alchemy” [II.4 ¶58]. At the close she describes her work as reviving “these lights and relics of the Sacred Art long buried in oblivion” [IV.4 ¶30], and holds that whoever “can understand the language of the philosophers, will understand their Art” [IV.4 ¶32].

The Platonic Successor (quoted) says Jupiter, after spontaneous revelation ceased, “has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance” [II.1 ¶53] for communication with the gods.

E1526.summary: A treatise cited for the labours of Hercules as the trials of whoever contends for liberty, and for the Spirit's sinking when the will inclines downward.
E1526.body: Atwood cites the Sacred Discourse in support: the labours of Hercules are the trials of whoever contends for liberty, and when the will inclines downward “the Spirit grows heavy and sinks into profound Hades” [II.2 ¶13–14].

E1527.summary: Sacred knowledge and rites which, too openly exposed to the multitude, became perverted and vilified.
E1527.body: Atwood: “sacred mysteries, too openly exposed to the multitude, became perverted and vilified by their abuse” [I.1 ¶11] — a ground for the secrecy she defends.

E1528.summary: In a quoted adept, the name for the genuine art which fraudulent books blasphemed.
E1528.body: Quoted from the adept, on fraudulent writers: “they have blasphemed the Sacred Science, and by their errors have brought contempt on men philosophizing” [I.1 ¶53].

E1529.summary: An anonymous voice whose sayings Atwood cites on sense-life, the purified internal fire, and putrefaction.
E1529.body: Atwood reads the sage's saying “Visitabis interiora terrae rectificando” [II.3 ¶28–29] (ours: you will visit the interior of the earth by rectifying) as referring to sense-life. Another saying supports the superiority of the purified internal fire: “Si pariat ventum valet auri pondera centum” [III.1 ¶43] (ours: if it brings forth wind, it is worth a hundred weights of gold). Via Ripley Revived, 5th Gate, the sage/adept supports putrefaction as the key, and tincture as coagulated blood: “O happy gate of blackness” [I.3 n42, n43].

E1530.summary: The voice of the Book of Enoch, cited to illustrate the guarded mineral soul.
E1530.body: Atwood cites the Book of Enoch, chap. 64: 7, 8: “there is an angel standing upon it, and that angel struggles to prevail” [II.3 ¶29; II.3 n32], illustrating the guarded mineral soul.

E1531.summary: Author of a two-volume work on the Mysteries whom Atwood criticizes as thorough in research but astronomical and superficial in reading.
E1531.body: Atwood cites Sainte Croix's des Mysteres (2 vols, 8vo) and criticizes it: the research is thorough, but the reading of the Mysteries is astronomical and superficial [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n2].

E1532.summary: Invoked for their gift of healing, which Atwood notes is absent today.
E1532.body: Atwood contrasts the saints and apostles' gift of healing with its absence today, promising the reason in the sequel [III.1 ¶9].

E1534.summary: Salt of the Wise (our rendering): Atwood's name for what arises when the hidden Reason is awakened, identified with Mercurius Philosophorum.
E1534.body: Atwood: “This is the Sal Sepientum et Mercurius Philosophorum” [II.4 ¶39] — so = Mercurius Philosophorum. The rendering Salt of the Wise is ours. In context it names what arises when the hidden Reason is awakened.

E1535.summary: In quoted adepts, an image of the Stone as born and nourished in fire, enduring it unharmed and curing diseases of men and metals.
E1535.body: The fraternity of the Rosy Cross (quoted) says the Eagle and Lion together take on the Salamander's nature, “which, if it remains in the fire without any detriment, cures all the diseases of men and metals” [III.3 ¶63]. Eudoxus (quoted) uses it as an image of the Stone, which “as a true Salamander receives it nativity, is nourished and grows in the Elementary Fire” [IV.3 ¶16].
